summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws in the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded the position publicly, stating that "there is nothing we can do." The decriminalisation arrived by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly.

The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, including its 2025 single-sex-services code, does not automatically apply in the British Virgin Islands. The territory stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume the Equality Act's discrimination and service-access protections are available there by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.

Family status remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid under British Virgin Islands law was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not itself a ruling on whether such a marriage is recognised in the territory.
tangentialFactors:
GlobalGayz rates the British Virgin Islands among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean in material published in 2012 and 2017, while describing native homophobia there as "silent and invisible" and gay life as lived in secret. The account concerns gay and lesbian residents and visitors rather than trans people specifically, and it describes social climate rather than legal standing. Read alongside the legal position, it suggests that open non-conformity may attract less overt hostility than elsewhere in the region while remaining largely invisible in public life.

The route to decriminalisation itself is evidence about local political conditions: the sodomy laws were struck down in 2001 by an order of the United Kingdom's Privy Council after the local legislature declined to act, and the change was imposed from outside rather than initiated locally.
localsOnly:
Residents of the British Virgin Islands conduct their family lives under a framework in which same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in January 2001 by order of the United Kingdom's Privy Council after the House of Assembly declined to legislate. The extension of United Kingdom statutes to the territory depends on Order in Council, so residents cannot invoke the Equality Act 2010 in local proceedings unless the United Kingdom has specifically extended it.

Resident couples are directly affected by the unresolved validity litigation. The United Kingdom marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome remains under challenge in the territory's courts, and the BVI Christian Council's failed bid of 29 July 2022 to appeal Justice Adrian Jack's case-management orders left those orders in force. Recognition of marriages celebrated outside the territory therefore remains unsettled pending the court's determination on the substantive question.

The inventory sources no local enactment extending to residents protections equivalent to the Equality Act 2010, and none extending the United Kingdom's same-sex marriage provisions to the British Virgin Islands.
outOfScopeNotes:
No provision on legal gender recognition, or on amending gender markers on British Virgin Islands identity documents or on the British passport issued there, is sourced in this inventory. How an amended marker would be read at entry to the territory is not established here.

Nothing in the inventory covers gender identity within the territory's hate-crime or sentencing framework, nor any local anti-discrimination statute addressing gender identity in employment, housing, health care or public services. Whether a comparable local statute exists is not resolved by these sources.

Rules governing access to sex-segregated facilities, and any local code on single-sex services, are not sourced, nor is access to gender-affirming health care or the treatment of trans people by the territory's police and courts. Constitutional protections for trans residents under the territory's own constitution are likewise not addressed.

The validity of same-sex marriages celebrated outside the British Virgin Islands remains unresolved in this inventory. The only sourced ruling is the 29 July 2022 refusal of the BVI Christian Council's bid to appeal Justice Adrian Jack's case-management orders, not a determination of the underlying question.
